title: Why Do Humans Tell Stories?
paragraphs: No known human culture is without stories. Whether in the form of myths, folk tales, novels or streaming series, storytelling is one of the most universal ways in which people share experience, pass on values and simply enjoy themselves.

For most of our history, stories were transmitted orally. Long before writing existed, communities relied on storytellers to preserve their history, explain the natural world and teach rules of behaviour. Rhythm, repetition and vivid characters made these stories easier to memorise and retell.

When writing appeared, some of these traditions were recorded. The Epic of Gilgamesh, written in ancient Mesopotamia, is often described as one of the earliest great works of literature. Its central concerns, friendship, grief and the search for meaning in the face of death, remain strikingly relevant.

Researchers have suggested several reasons why stories are so powerful. Information embedded in a narrative tends to be remembered better than isolated facts, because stories link events through cause and emotion. Stories also invite us to see the world through someone else’s eyes, and some studies indicate that reading fiction is associated with a greater ability to understand others’ feelings, although the evidence is still debated.
